cur:catacombs2-marseille-saint-victor-ch.summary: At the centre of this low relief, Christ sits enthroned within a circular medallion borne by two winged genii, an open book in his hand. At the ends Paul, at the left, and Peter, carrying a cross, turn towards him in acclamation. The flat, linear carving in local stone shows the transformation of Roman funerary sculpture in fifth-century Provence.
facts: Only fragments survive; the sarcophagus was reconstituted with the help of old drawings.
The medallion carried by winged figures adapts the imago clipeata, the shield-portrait of the deceased on Roman sarcophagi, to the figure of Christ.
cur:catacombs2-marseille-saint-victor-ch.notes: Parts of the relief are restorations based on drawings.

Q1825931.summary: Christ hangs on a jewelled cross at the centre of this golden cover, his body upright and calm, set against fields crowded with great raised clusters of gems. Small repoussé figures crouch or hover in the compartments around the cross: angels above its arms, and below them the Virgin and St John, each paired with another mourner. The Crucifixion is presented not as defeat but as glory, the cross transformed into a jewelled throne.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the upper cover is late Carolingian work of about 880, while the older lower cover is Insular-style work of the later 8th century, probably made in modern Austria.

Scholars disagree about the two extra mourning women below the cross: the Morgan Library's notes call them personifications of Christian souls, Peter Lasko a duplicated Mary Magdalene, and Paul Needham Mary Magdalene and Mary Cleophas.
When J. P. Morgan bought the book in 1901 it was his first major purchase of a medieval manuscript.

cur:objects-ratchis-altar.summary: On the front of this Lombard altar Christ sits frontally within a mandorla carried by four flying angels, holding a book and blessing, while cherubim appear beside him. The flat, linear carving and the large heads and hands of the figures are typical of Lombard sculpture. The sides show the Visitation and the Adoration of the Magi, so that the altar unites the Incarnation with the glory of Christ.
facts: The altar is dated 737–744, while Ratchis, son of Duke Pemmo, ruled Friuli before becoming king of the Lombards in 744 (Wikipedia; museum dating recorded with the photographs).
The relief was originally painted; the museum presents a multimedia reconstruction of its original colours.

walters:W.432.62R.summary: Judas, in a green tunic and red cloak, embraces Christ and presses his face to his, while soldiers close in from behind with raised weapons. At the left, Peter lifts his sword over the fallen servant, Malchus, on the ground. Placed in the midst of John's account of Peter's denial, the miniature recalls the betrayal that set the Passion in motion.
facts: The miniature sits within the text of John 18 in this Leiden prayer book, next to the account of Peter warming himself and denying Christ.
The Walters records that the manuscript was owned by Edwin H. Lawrence (sold 1892), W. C. Hazlitt and Marshall C. Lefferts before coming to Henry Walters.
